$comment-tag-format: include-component-in-tag MUST stay false, and it is the setting most likely to be dropped when copying this file: nothing about it looks load-bearing. With it absent, release-please defaults to true and names the tag `kartikeya-v0.1.0` instead of `v0.1.0`. release.yml triggers on `v*`, which that does not match — so the tag would be created and nothing would publish, with no error anywhere. That exact mistake was made on willow-mcp#256. tests/test_release_wiring.py checks the produced tag against the workflow trigger, because a comment did not stop it happening once.
$comment-first-bump: The next feat: takes this from 0.0.9 to 0.1.0, not 0.0.10 — 0.0.x forever conveys nothing. A breaking change takes it to 1.0.0, because bump-minor-pre-major is FALSE. bump-patch-for-minor-pre-major false keeps fix: at a patch. Verified against release-please 17.11.1 rather than inferred: at 0.0.9, breaking -> 1.0.0, feat -> 0.1.0, fix -> 0.0.10. Note the version itself is tag-derived (hatch-vcs), so nothing in the tree needs bumping to match — which is why there are no extra-files here, unlike willow-mcp. WHY IT CHANGED. The flag used to be true, keeping a breaking change at a minor so that reaching 1.0 stayed a deliberate decision. Dependents paid for that: a `<1.0.0` cap accepted every version this config could produce, so it promised nothing. willow-mcp tried `kartikeya>=0.0.9,<0.1.0` to close it downstream and withdrew it — that cap would have expired on the very next feat: commit, the one described above, and a tight cap blocks a producer's security patches while still missing an unlabelled breaking `refactor:`, which bumps a patch. Yes, this means 0.0.9 goes straight to 1.0.0 on the first breaking change. That is the point: the number then says what happened. WHAT STILL IS NOT GUARANTEED: this keys off the commit type, so a break mislabelled as `refactor:` still ships as a patch. Dependents catch that with a contract test against the really-installed package — see willow-mcp's docs/design/fleet-versioning.md Rule 1.
$comment-what-cuts-a-release: EVERY type listed above without "hidden": true cuts a release on its own — not just feat and fix. jeles learned this the expensive way: v0.4.1 was tagged and published to PyPI for a single ci: commit that changed a workflow file and nothing a user installs. That is survivable while release PRs are merged by hand, because you see what is in them; release-please.yml here arms auto-merge, so an un-hidden type ships to PyPI unattended, and a PyPI version can never be reused.
$comment-hidden-rule: The line is: does this commit change what someone gets from `pip install kartikeya`? docs/test/ci do not — tests and workflows are not packaged, and a README edit only moves the PyPI page — so they are hidden and ride along with the next real release. build and deps stay visible because a dependency or packaging change genuinely alters the installed artifact, and hiding them would mean a dependency fix never reaching anyone, silently. refactor and perf stay visible because they change shipped code, and a version number is what you point at when a refactor turns out to have broken something. Hidden also means absent from CHANGELOG.md — release-please has no 'list it but do not release on it' setting, so this is a real trade, taken deliberately.
